summary: In the conch of the main apse of the New Church, Christ hangs on a tall cross against a deep blue sky, his head bowed and his body slack in death, between the grieving Virgin and Saint John; the soldiers with lance and sponge and further mourners stand below, and angels and the sun and moon appear above the arms of the cross. Placing the Crucifixion directly over the altar, rather than a majestic Christ, made the sacrifice commemorated at every liturgy the visual centre of the church.
facts: The New Church was cut out of the east wall of the earlier Old Church and is famous for its intense blue backgrounds, painted with costly ultramarine made from lapis lazuli.

An inscription in the north apse names a painter, Nikephoros, and the patrons Constantine and his son Leo; Ann Wharton Epstein argued that Nikephoros' workshop was responsible for the whole decoration of the New Church.

links.label: UNESCO: Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia

notes: Dating of the New Church varies in the literature from the mid-10th century (Epstein: 'tenth-century metropolitan art') to the end of the 10th or early 11th century.

summary: Christ, haloed and robed in blue, reclines at the left end of a semicircular table while the apostles crowd in a curving row behind it; a single large red chalice-like dish stands at the centre of the green tabletop. The scene belongs to the Passion register of the Old Church's barrel-vault cycle, painted in the pale reds and greens that distinguish the Old Church from the later, blue New Church.
facts: The Old Church vault carries one of the fullest Christological cycles in Cappadocia: on each side three registers show the Infancy, the Miracles and the Passion, with a spine of prophet medallions along the crown of the vault.
The sigma-shaped (semicircular) table with Christ reclining at one end follows the ancient banqueting arrangement used in early Christian and Byzantine images of the Last Supper.

summary: The Holy Family journeys from left to right in a frieze of haloed figures: the Virgin rides the donkey with the Christ Child, accompanied by Joseph and a young companion who leads the way. Drawn in soft reds and greens on a pale ground, the scene is part of the Infancy register of the Old Church vault, where the narrative closely follows apocryphal as well as canonical sources.
facts: The Old Church cycle draws on the Protevangelium (Gospel) of James as well as the canonical Gospels; it continues the Infancy story beyond the Flight into Egypt with the Murder of Zacharias and the Flight of Elizabeth.
Cappadocian painters often show a youth leading the donkey, identified in Byzantine tradition as James, Joseph's son from his first marriage.
notes: The photographer identifies the leading figure as St James the brother of the Lord; this is consistent with Byzantine iconography but was not confirmed from an inscription.

summary: Against a brilliant blue ground the Virgin lies on a mattress beside the manger in which the swaddled Christ Child rests, while a host of angels bends over the scene from above; in the lower part two midwives prepare the Child's first bath. The deep ultramarine and the elegant, well-modelled figures are characteristic of the New Church's sophisticated workshop.
facts: The bathing of the newborn Christ by midwives, drawn from apocryphal tradition, became a standard part of Byzantine Nativity images, affirming the reality of the Incarnation.
The same composition appears in another Commons photograph labelled as Tokalı Kilise (TOKALIKILISE 057), which confirms the location of this unlabelled image.
notes: The Commons file has no location in its description and dates the painting to the 12th century; it is categorised under the Tokalı frescoes and matches a located photograph of the New Church Nativity, so the 10th-century date of the New Church is used here.

summary: The Virgin sits enthroned at the left holding the Christ Child on her lap, while the three Magi, crowned and richly dressed, advance in a tight group from the right bearing their gifts; Joseph and an angel stand behind. A Greek inscription runs across the blue sky above the figures.
facts: The Magi are shown as three ages of man (young, mature and old), a convention widely used in Byzantine art to suggest that all humanity comes to worship Christ.
notes: The Commons file is unlabelled ('The magi. Fresco in Cappadocia', dated there to the 12th century) but is categorised among the Tokalı Kilise frescoes; the blue ground and style indicate the New Church. Location should be treated as probable.

summary: Christ stands at the centre on a green ground, bearded and haloed, in a blue tunic and brown mantle, stretching out both hands over the apostles who bow towards him in two tiers on either side; slender trees frame him and Greek inscriptions are written on the blue sky. The image of the risen Lord commissioning his disciples is one of the most celebrated in the New Church, where the Mission of the Apostles occupies a prominent place in the nave vault.
facts: In the New Church a few key scenes – the Ascension, the Benediction of the Apostles, Pentecost and the Mission of the Apostles – were given the prominent central and southern bays of the nave vault.
The bowing apostles are arranged in overlapping rows so that their haloes form rhythmic diagonal lines converging on Christ.
notes: The Commons file is unlabelled ('Jesus and apostles. Fresco in Cappadocia', dated there to the 12th century) but is categorised among the Tokalı Kilise frescoes. Whether it shows the Mission or the Benediction of the Apostles (both are in the New Church vault) was not confirmed from the inscriptions.

summary: Christ sits frontally on a high-backed jewelled throne with a cushion, a large cross-inscribed halo behind his head, holding a richly bound Gospel book on his knee and raising his right hand in blessing. Much of the paint of the face and mantle has worn away, but the monumental pose of the Ruler of All remains clear.
facts: Enthroned images of Christ holding the Gospel book were often placed in apses or flanked by the Virgin and John the Baptist in a Deesis, as intercession for the faithful.
notes: The photograph is labelled only 'Christ Pantocrator scene'; its exact position within Tokalı Kilise (Old or New Church) was not verified, so a general 10th-century date is given.

summary: At the centre of the small cut-rock dome, Christ rises within a circular mandorla of concentric bands, borne up by angels whose wings spread around it, while the apostles stand in a ring of pale-robed figures below. Framed by bands of ornament, the whole cupola becomes an image of heaven opening above the worshipper.
facts: The church takes its popular name, 'Church under the Tree', from its setting in the Ihlara gorge; it is also called the Church of Daniel after a painting of Daniel between the lions facing the entrance.
English Wikipedia describes the Ascension in the cupola as pre-Iconoclast, while other sources date the paintings to the 9th–11th centuries; their unusual, schematic style makes them hard to date.
notes: Date disputed: proposals range from the 7th century (pre-Iconoclast) to the 10th–11th century.

summary: On a yellow ground framed by a white border, the Virgin sits on a pale donkey holding the Christ Child before her, while Joseph, leaning on a staff, walks at the left and a second haloed figure leads the animal at the right. Surrounded by losses in the plaster, this small panel near the dome preserves the simple, flat colours characteristic of the church.
facts: The paintings of Ağaçaltı combine figure scenes with dense geometric and textile-like ornament, one of the reasons scholars have found them difficult to date.
notes: Date disputed: proposals range from the 7th century to the 10th–11th century. The faces are damaged and modern graffiti are scratched into the lower part.

summary: Two surviving fragments preserve the upper part of the Virgin's mantle and, at the top, the Christ Child seated on her arm: a frontal boy with large dark eyes and a cross-inscribed halo, holding a scroll and blessing. Below, the Virgin's long purple-brown robe falls in heavy vertical folds to a footstool. The type, in which Mary presents her Son to the viewer, is known as the Hodegetria, 'she who shows the way'.
facts: The painting was removed from the walls of Faras Cathedral during the Polish excavations of 1961–64 directed by Kazimierz Michałowski, part of the UNESCO Nubian Campaign before the area was flooded by Lake Nasser.
The National Museum in Warsaw holds 67 paintings from Faras; the cathedral's walls bore several superimposed layers of painting from the 7th to the 14th century.

links.label: National Museum in Warsaw – Digital Museum record
Wikipedia: Faras Gallery at the National Museum in Warsaw

summary: Only fragments survive: at the right the white, red-striped robe and bare feet of the standing risen Christ, with his hand extended, and at the left the red-mantled figure of Mary Magdalene bending low before him; above, parts of a haloed head and another white garment remain. Even in ruins the encounter in the garden – the first appearance of the risen Lord – can be read in the contrast of the upright Christ and the kneeling woman.
facts: The museum identifies the scene as the resurrected Christ with Mary Magdalene; it comes from Faras Cathedral, excavated by the Polish expedition in 1961–64.

links.label: National Museum in Warsaw – Digital Museum record
Wikipedia: Faras Gallery at the National Museum in Warsaw

notes: Very fragmentary; identification follows the National Museum in Warsaw. Date range straddles AD 1000.

summary: On a dark grey ground at the left, a large haloed figure – its paint largely lost, so that it survives mainly as a pale silhouette – reaches down to a tangle of small naked figures rising from the depths, the souls of the dead freed from Hades. At the right, against a glowing orange ground, a smaller standing figure in a pale robe completes the composition above a band of interlace.
facts: Banganarti, near Old Dongola, the capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, was excavated by Polish archaeologists, who recovered a large body of wall paintings from its churches.
notes: Identification and date follow the photographer's Commons description ('Harrowing of Hell, turn of 11th cent., today in Poznań'). Christ's figure is largely effaced; the identification is consistent with the composition but could not be confirmed from a museum record.

summary: The Virgin, wrapped in a dark brown mantle, reclines diagonally on a great patterned mattress strewn with rosettes, beside a gridded structure representing the manger and stable in which the swaddled Child lay; at the left the shepherds and other small figures approach, one in a yellow robe. The painting is badly abraded, and the Child himself is now barely legible within the manger.
facts: Abdallah Nirqi was one of the Lower Nubian sites investigated during the UNESCO campaign of the 1960s before its flooding by Lake Nasser.
notes: Facts follow the Commons description (Nativity, church of Abdallah Nirqi, 10th century, Coptic Museum, Cairo); not confirmed against a museum record. The Christ Child is very faint in the photograph.

summary: In the semidome of a niche in the east wall, Christ sits enthroned within a circular glory surrounded by the four living creatures; in the zone below, the Virgin stands at the centre among a row of apostles. This two-tier composition – Christ in glory above, Mary and the apostles on earth below – is the classic Egyptian monastic apse image, recorded here on an old glass slide soon after the excavations at Bawit.
facts: Bawit's chapels were excavated by Jean Clédat and Émile Chassinat at the beginning of the 20th century; many paintings recorded then were later lost or removed.
The slide's handwritten label reads 'Baouit. Salle 20. Niche du mur Est. Ensemble'.
notes: Image is a historical photograph (EuroPhot glass slide, Commons description says 'before restoration'); the painting's present location or survival was not verified.

summary: In this detail from a niche painting, the Virgin, with large dark eyes and a halo, looks out frontally from her throne, holding the small Christ Child before her breast; the Greek abbreviations for 'Mother of God' flank her head. The direct, wide-eyed gaze is typical of the icon-like monastic paintings of Bawit.
facts: The slide's handwritten label identifies the painting as the Virgin in the niche of Room 30 ('Baouit. Salle 30. Niche de la Vierge, détail').
Enthroned Virgins with the Child were frequent in the prayer niches of the monks' cells at Bawit and Saqqara.
notes: Historical photograph (EuroPhot glass slide); an overall view of the niche is also on Commons (GDE000855).

summary: Within a painted niche crowned by an arch of medallion busts, the Virgin sits enthroned and turns slightly as she offers her breast to the Christ Child, who leans in from the left, gripping her with both hands. The tender, unusual subject of the nursing Mother of God – the Galaktotrophousa – appears here in one of its earliest monumental examples.
facts: The photograph comes from J. E. Quibell's excavation report, Excavations at Saqqara (1908–9, 1909–10): The Monastery of Apa Jeremias, published in 1912.

The Egyptian image of the nursing Virgin is often compared with earlier Egyptian depictions of Isis nursing Horus, though the Christian image carries its own theological meaning: the true humanity of the Son of God.

links.label: Internet Archive: Quibell, Excavations at Saqqara (1912)

notes: Present location not verified from a museum record (the main Saqqara wall paintings were transferred to the Coptic Museum, Cairo). Dating of the Saqqara cell paintings varies between the 6th and 8th centuries.

summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a jewelled throne with the Christ Child on her lap, both looking straight out; two youthful archangels raise their hands in acclamation on either side, and two elderly saints stand at the ends, one holding a book. Fragmentary Greek or Coptic labels survive above the heads. The flat, brightly coloured figures are known here through the colour plate of the 1912 excavation report.
facts: The picture is a colour plate from Quibell's 1912 report on the Monastery of Apa Jeremias, whose monks' cells were decorated with prayer-niche paintings of Christ, the Virgin and the monastery's founders.

links.label: Internet Archive: Quibell, Excavations at Saqqara (1912)

notes: The image is a 1912 colour reproduction rather than a photograph. The inscription at the left appears to begin with the name of Apa Jeremias, but the saints' identities were not confirmed.

summary: On a pier of the basilica, the Virgin, veiled in a dark maphorion, and Saint Theodore, bearded and in a white chlamys, stand in prayer against a blue ground; between them, a small bust of Christ appears in a segment of heaven at the top, from which rays descend towards them. The Virgin holds an inscribed scroll interceding with her Son, making this panel a precious early image of prayer addressed to Christ through his Mother and the saints.
facts: Hagios Demetrios is famous for its group of pre-Iconoclast mosaic panels on the piers and walls; many others were destroyed in the Great Thessaloniki Fire of 1917.

links.label: UNESCO: Paleochristian and Byzantine Monuments of Thessaloniki

notes: Usually grouped with the 7th-century pier mosaics; a Commons file of the same panel gives a 9th-century date. The text of the scroll was not transcribed here.

summary: In the conch of a small apse, Christ stands frontally on a deep blue ground, haloed and holding a jewelled Gospel book, blessing in the Greek manner; the two deacon-martyrs Lawrence and Stephen, in light robes, turn towards him from either side. The image crowns a crypt whose walls also show the martyrdoms of these two saints.
facts: The crypt was painted for Abbot Epiphanius (824–842), who appears as a kneeling donor beside the Crucifixion on another wall of the same small chamber.
Lawrence and Stephen, both deacons and early martyrs, were often paired in Roman and Benedictine devotion.

summary: On the vault of the crypt a bearded, haloed Christ sits within an oval glory, blessing with his right hand and holding a book, his mantle painted in warm ochres. The surface is faded and worn, but the figure's calm frontality makes it the spiritual centre of the little chapel.
facts: The paintings are attributed to a Benedictine workshop working for Abbot Epiphanius (824–842), under whom the abbey grew to more than 300 monks; the area of the crypt was re-excavated by the San Vincenzo Project from 1980.

summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a jewelled throne set within a large circular glory, with the Christ Child, golden-haloed, held before her; below, a row of saints' heads looks out. The full composition, of which this is the upper part, also includes a monk kneeling in adoration – a reminder of the community for whom the crypt was painted.
facts: The crypt combines images of Christ, the Virgin, the Annunciation and Nativity with the martyrdoms of Lawrence and Stephen, a programme focused on intercession for the abbot and his monks.
notes: The kneeling monk mentioned in the Commons title is not visible in this crop.

summary: The newborn Christ, a sturdy child with a golden cross-nimbus, sits upright in a large footed basin shaped like a chalice, while a midwife seated at the left tests the water and a second woman at the right pours from a jug. Part of the crypt's Nativity, the scene's eucharistic overtones – the Child in a chalice-like font – would have been clear to the monks who prayed here.
facts: The bathing of the Child by midwives comes from apocryphal tradition and was a standard part of Nativity images in both Byzantine and Western early medieval art.

summary: The apse conch preserves the lower half of a monumental theophany: the lower body and jewelled footstool of the enthroned Christ, radiating lines of glory, and, at the sides, fiery wheels and wings of the heavenly powers that surround him. The upper part with Christ's head has been lost, yet the painting remains one of the rare surviving 7th-century church murals in Armenia.
facts: Lmbatavank is a small cruciform domed church of the 7th century dedicated to Saint Stephen; its apse frescoes show 'Jesus in the center surrounded by symbols of heavenly powers'.
A painting of Saint George on horseback holding a cross-topped staff also survives in the church.
notes: Christ's figure survives only below the waist; identification of the theophany follows Wikipedia.
